note: Valdez & Valdez (BIFEA 2000) and Wikipedia place Incaraqay on the summit of Alkowillka (Allqu Willka) only as a site of the Inka period; no source gives a year, century or millennium for its start.

Wikipedia calls Lee Wood an Iron Age enclosure or hill fort and mentions Neolithic ashes in a fireplace under its bank, but gives no year or century for the fort's construction; the enclosure is unexcavated.

The Portuguese article, the national register and the Portal do Arqueologo date the dam only as romana / período romano, and no source gives a year, century or millennium for its construction, so the field stays empty.

The only printed coordinates are the Spanish Wikipedia/Wikidata point (-13.5704, -71.9957), which lies south-west of Cusco and contradicts the MINCETUR inventory and both Wikipedias placing Cheqollo north of San Jeronimo, 3 km from its plaza; the inventory gives no coordinates, so no source gives the site's point.

The district page of Kizilcahamam.bel.tr describes the site only in words (village 18 km from the district centre, caves, rock churches) and embeds the location solely in a Google Maps frame; no coordinate is printed in the page's visible text, so nothing can be quoted for the site's point.

The same page only speculates that the residents of the caves 'were the first Christians that lived in hiding' and gives no year, century or millennium for the start of the site, so no source dates it.
The sources give only the city's role in the Latin/Samnite wars and its destruction (340 or 314 BC); none dates its foundation or first occupation.

No source gives a year or century for the founding of Pisarissos: English Wikipedia says only that it was 'inhabited during Roman times' and that its name 'is inferred by epigraphic and other evidence', which is a period word, not a dated start. The field stays empty.

A natural park has no ancient start: the park's dates (1979, Law 5/2000) are its designation, and the Dacian fortresses and caves inside it are separate sites, so no source dates this park's own beginning.

The MINCETUR inventory record says only that occupation may go back to the Periodo Intermedio Tardio (Killke) and that the site belongs to the Inca period; no year or century is given, and period words alone do not date a site.

No source I could read prints a point for the Al-Dafi site itself: the English Wikipedia article carries an infobox map frame with missing coordinates and no P625 statement exists in the Wikidata item Q22690291. The stored point 25.4297, 49.6219 sits in the Al-Ahsa oasis, while the article places Al-Dafi near Jubail, but nothing quotable gives the site's own coordinates, so the point stays as it is for the owner.

The only point a source prints is Serbian Wikipedia's 42.8117, 21.2003, which lies about 11 km from the stored point and does not agree with the article's own description of the site as southeast of Balovac either; no source can be quoted for the site's point, so the stored point stands and the site goes to the owner's list.

Neither the English nor the Serbian article dates the site: they describe the trapezoidal fortification, its cut stone and brick ramparts and the 1986 protection date, but give no year, century or millennium for the start of occupation.

English Wikipedia says only that the oldest tombs are from the Bronze Age (a period word) and that the oldest graves of the southern necropolis, one part of the group, date to 350 BC; no source dates the start of the necropolises as a whole.
No readable source prints a point for the lost Cossington sarsen group; Wikipedia gives none and the Megalithic Portal refuses automated requests.
Wikipedia says only 'Neolithic' (a period word, and hedged as a possible long barrow); no source gives a year or century.

Wikipedia prints no coordinates (only 'near today's village of Komin'). Pleiades 197461 gives a 1:1M-scale DARMC point (46.002444, 16.2846) within 1 km of the stored point, but its HTML page is behind an Anubis bot challenge and the JSON prints longitude first, so no quotable coordinate text can be cited.

Wikipedia only calls it an ancient Roman settlement; Pleiades gives only the Roman/late-antique period range (30 BC - AD 640) for the name attestation, which is a period word, not a dated start of the site.
No source found dates Hatun Usnu.

No readable source gives a point for this museum. The Arabic Wikipedia article on it carries no coordinate template, no Wikidata item exists for the site, a Nominatim lookup for the site name returns nothing, and the points that search surfaces (34.56000N 38.26722E on merefa.org) belong to the city of Palmyra as a whole and come from a Wikipedia mirror, which is refused. The stored point stays as it is and the site goes to the owner's list.

The source that describes the site, the Arabic Wikipedia article, calls it a museum in Arabic (متحف) only, and no page I found names it in Latin script, so I cannot supply a quote the checker can read that holds a word of the type. The type is very probably Museum, but a field no checkable source supports stays as it is and goes to the owner.

The only page about this very museum that I could read is its Arabic Wikipedia article, which names the site in Arabic only; no English or other Latin-script page about this museum exists that I could find, and the UNESCO page for the Site of Palmyra is about the whole site and cannot be read. Since I cannot quote a page that names the site in a form the check accepts, the field stays empty and goes to the owner.

Sources say only that the site belongs to the Mature Harappan phase (a period word); the DOAM chronology 3500 BCE - 1800 BCE is a generic span shared by many Proto Historic records and contradicts the Mature Harappan attribution, and no readable source gives a year for the start of this site.
No readable source prints a point for T'uqu T'uquyuq: Wikipedia and Wikidata carry none, and the only point found (an OpenStreetMap node via Mapcarta) is not quotable in the required form.
No source dates T'uqu T'uquyuq; only a travel page says the Saywa rock paintings are up to 4,000 years old, which is not a dated start for this site.
No readable source dates the start of the Te Pito Kura ahu itself; the only date found (Paro erected around 1620) dates one statue, not the site's construction or first use.

The sources date the site's phases only as periods, not as a calendar year: the English Wikipedia infobox lists 'Periods Late Bronze Age First Iron Age' and dates only the end ('History Abandoned c. 550 BC'), and the text says the site 'presents a continuous occupation since the Last Bronze Age' - a period word, not a year. The OpenEdition study of protohistoric construction techniques names Barranc de Gàfols as an example of Iron Age house-block sites but dates the technique, not this site's start. An abandonment date is not a start, and the rules exclude a period word alone, so no source gives a year, century or millennium for the start and the field stays empty.
Wikipedia (en, es) gives no date for Isog, only its location and the 1956-57 excavations; no source dates its start.
The MINCETUR record classes the site as Ciudadelas and describes dwellings, storehouses and ritual use, but no readable source states a canonical type in words the quote check can match.
No readable source prints a point for Huichún: the English Wikipedia article and its Wikidata item carry no coordinates and the tourism-inventory page is not readable.
No source found gives a date for the start of Huichún; Wikipedia only gives its 2006 heritage declaration.
The English Wikipedia article locates the site and explains the Quechua name ('ancient place') but gives no year, century or millennium for its construction or first occupation.
